hooks.text: A dying spacecraft survived its trip to Mercury by sailing on sunlight.
How did a broken space probe steal speed from Venus to reach Mercury?
Three flybys of Mercury saved a failing mission running entirely out of gas.

title: The Broken Probe That Sailed on Sunlight to Mercury
description: Discover how Mariner 10 overcame relentless breakdowns and used a gravity assist past Venus to reach Mercury.

beats.text: A dying spacecraft survived its trip to Mercury by sailing on sunlight.
beats.visual: artist concept of Mariner 10 spacecraft angling solar panels in space, 1973

beats.text: In November 1973, NASA launched Mariner 10 to attempt the very first interplanetary gravity assist.
beats.visual: Atlas-Centaur launch of Mariner 10 from Cape Canaveral, 1973

beats.text: Soon after takeoff, camera heaters failed and peeling paint tricked the star-tracker into losing its guide star.
When attitude control gas ran critically low, engineers gambled on a completely untested maneuver.
beats.visual: diagram illustrating the Venus gravity assist trajectory to Mercury, 1974

beats.text: Controllers angled the solar panels to catch the pressure of solar radiation, using sunlight itself as a rudder.
beats.visual: artist concept of solar pressure navigation on Mariner 10, 1974

beats.text: That brilliant improvised fix let Venus fling the probe toward Mercury for three historic flybys.
beats.visual: Mariner 10 first close-up mosaic of Mercury, 1974

beats.text: Without that sunlight-driven escape, no broken ship could ever sail across the inner solar system.
beats.visual: Mariner 10 flight spare on display at the National Air and Space Museum, 1975
